what_its_for: Amivantamab-vmjw is a cancer medicine used to treat a type of lung cancer called non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). It is used when your lung cancer has certain changes (mutations) in a gene called EGFR, specifically insertions in exon 20. It may also be used for other EGFR or MET mutation-related lung cancers as directed by your doctor. This medicine works by targeting and blocking proteins on cancer cells that help them grow.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion directly into your vein by a healthcare professional in a clinic or hospital setting. You will NOT give this medicine to yourself at home. Each infusion session may take several hours, so plan your day accordingly. You will be given medicines before each infusion (such as antihistamines, fever reducers, and steroids) to help prevent or reduce infusion reactions. Stay at the clinic for monitoring after each infusion as instructed by your healthcare team.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your body weight. Doses are typically given once a week for the first 4 weeks, then once every 2 weeks after that, as part of your treatment plan. Your doctor may slow down, pause, or permanently stop your infusions depending on how you respond or if you have side effects. Never adjust your own dosing schedule — always follow your doctor's instructions.
missed_dose: Since this medicine is given to you by a healthcare professional, it is very important to keep all of your scheduled clinic appointments. If you miss or need to reschedule an infusion appointment, call your doctor or clinic right away so they can reschedule you as soon as possible. Do not wait until your next scheduled appointment without contacting your healthcare team first.
storage: You will not store this medicine at home. It is prepared and stored by healthcare professionals at the clinic or hospital. If you have any questions about storage, ask your pharmacist or nurse.
what_to_avoid: Avoid sun exposure as much as possible during treatment, especially on your face, since this medicine can cause serious skin reactions and rash. Use sunscreen (SPF 30 or higher), wear protective clothing, and wear a hat when going outside. Do not start any new prescription medicines, over-the-counter drugs, vitamins, or herbal supplements without first checking with your doctor or pharmacist, as some products may interact with your treatment. Avoid becoming pregnant during treatment and for at least 3 months after your last dose. Talk to your doctor about effective birth control options. If you are breastfeeding, discuss with your doctor before continuing, as this medicine may harm a nursing baby.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience any of the following: trouble breathing, shortness of breath, or a new cough (which may be signs of a serious lung problem called interstitial lung disease); severe skin rash, blistering, or peeling; chest pain or fast heartbeat during or after your infusion; signs of an infusion reaction such as chills, fever, flushing, dizziness, or feeling faint; swelling of your hands, feet, or face; eye problems such as redness, watering, blurred vision, or light sensitivity; severe or worsening skin reactions on your face, scalp, chest, or back; signs of infection such as fever over 100.4°F (38°C), chills, or painful skin sores. Contact your doctor promptly for any new or worsening symptoms, even if they seem minor.
when_it_works: Every patient responds differently to this medicine. Some people may begin to see benefits within the first few months of treatment, but it may take longer in others. Your doctor will regularly check how the medicine is working through imaging scans and blood tests. Continue attending all your appointments even if you feel well. Do not stop treatment without talking to your doctor first.
special_populations: Pregnancy: This medicine can harm an unborn baby. If you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant, tell your doctor immediately. Use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 3 months after your last dose. Breastfeeding: It is not known if this medicine passes into breast milk. Do not breastfeed during treatment and for at least 3 months after your last dose. Older adults (age 65 and older): This medicine can be used in older adults, but you may be more likely to experience certain side effects such as swelling or skin reactions. Your doctor will monitor you closely. Kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor if you have kidney or liver disease, as this may affect how you tolerate the medicine. Children: The safety and effectiveness of this medicine in children have not been established.
